text: AWS Application Load Balancer's 'least outstanding requests' algorithm sends each request to the target with the fewest in-progress requests; AWS recommends it when requests vary in complexity or targets vary in capacity.
why: Shows the production name and use-case of the least-connections idea.

text: nginx's least_conn takes server weights into account, and when several servers tie for the fewest active connections it tries them in weighted round-robin order.
why: Concrete tie-break rule from a real load balancer.

text: If every target in an AWS ALB target group fails its health checks, the load balancer fails open and routes to all targets regardless of health.
why: Removing every 'dead' backend would cause a total outage; real LBs guard against it.

text: AWS distinguishes liveness, local and dependency (deep) health checks. Deep checks that include a shared dependency such as the database can fail on every server at once and take the whole fleet out of service.
why: Explains the risk of making the health endpoint ping the DB.

text: Besides active health checks, nginx does passive checks: after max_fails failed attempts within fail_timeout (default 10 s) a server is marked unavailable for fail_timeout, so real request failures remove a dead backend between checks.
why: Shows how real LBs shrink the stale window without polling.

text: Redis Pub/Sub is at-most-once: if a subscriber is disconnected or errors, the message is lost. Redis Streams persist messages and support at-least-once delivery.
why: The design needs a durable path so no LB server keeps stale config.

text: Prometheus keeps data in its own local TSDB in two-hour blocks with a write-ahead log; local storage is single-node, and remote write sends samples to external clustered or durable stores.
why: Corrects the backend-store claim and shows how Prometheus scales storage.

text: Prometheus collects metrics by pulling (scraping) targets over HTTP; pushing is supported through an intermediary Pushgateway intended for short-lived jobs.
why: Pull vs push is a common interview point about Prometheus.

text: AWS ELB returns the IPs of its load balancer nodes via DNS; as traffic changes it scales and updates the DNS entry, using a 60-second TTL so IPs can be remapped quickly.
why: Real-world confirmation of the DNS-based LB scaling design, with the TTL used.

text: In Route 53 weighted routing a weight-0 record gets no traffic; if all non-zero records fail their health checks, Route 53 answers with the zero-weight records, giving active-passive failover.
why: Shows the weight-0 trick plus automatic failover.

text: Google's Maglev serves the same service IP from many machines: routers spread packets across Maglev machines with ECMP, and consistent hashing plus connection tracking keep each connection on one backend.
why: Shows how one IP can be served by many LB machines.

text: nginx 'hash $key consistent' uses ketama consistent hashing, so adding or removing a server remaps only a few keys; a plain hash can remap most keys.
why: Explains why consistent hashing matters for session affinity.

text: Standard Reserved Instances for Linux/UNIX can be modified to other sizes within the same instance family and generation, as long as the total instance-size footprint stays the same.
why: Practical remedy for mismatched RI purchases.

text: On Linux the ephemeral local port range defaults to 32768-60999, which bounds how many simultaneous connections one LB IP can open to a single backend ip:port (about 28k).
why: A real limit behind the 'LB server runs out of connections' argument.

text: AWS ALB uses connection multiplexing: requests from many client connections can share a single backend connection, so the number of open backend connections does not equal how busy a target is.
why: Explains why modern LBs count outstanding requests, not connections.

text: EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking lets you pick a metric such as ASGAverageCPUUtilization and a target (e.g. 50%); Auto Scaling creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms that trigger scale-out and scale-in.
why: Concrete version of 'configure a rule and the service queries metrics'.

text: ZooKeeper watches are one-time triggers delivered to the client that set them, and a client sees the watch event before it sees the new data; clients must re-register watches after each event.
why: Key detail if ZooKeeper replaces Redis Pub/Sub for config push.

text: For every scrape target Prometheus records 'up' = 1 if the target was reachable and 0 if the scrape failed.
why: Shows what health signal Prometheus gives for free.

text: gRPC's client-side weighted round robin computes per-backend weights from backend-reported utilization and QPS, delivered per call or out-of-band, so load-aware routing is possible without a query per request.
why: A practical way to use backend load without slowing the routing decision.

text: CoreDNS's loadbalance plugin acts as a round-robin DNS load balancer by randomizing the order of A, AAAA and MX records in each answer.
why: Shows exactly how much 'balancing' CoreDNS does.

text: AWS ALB can authenticate users through an OIDC identity provider or Amazon Cognito before forwarding, passing signed user claims to targets in the x-amzn-oidc-data header.
why: Authentication can be offloaded to the LB even though authorization stays in the service.
